stem: A college endowment pays Rs 9,000 every six months to a scholarship fund, in perpetuity. If the annual discount rate is 12% compounded semi-annually, what is the present value of this perpetuity?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Uses the annual rate 12% without halving: 9000 / 0.12 = 75,000, ignoring that payments are semi-annual.
Annualises the payment to 18,000 and divides by 12%: 18000 / 0.12 = 1,50,000... but here a student uses 10% by mistake: 18000 / 0.10 = 1,80,000.
Treats the semi-annual payment as annual and uses 9%: 9000 / 0.09 = 1,00,000, merging wrong rate conversion with wrong period.

explanation: When payments and compounding are both semi-annual, the perpetuity formula still applies but the rate must match the payment period.

explanation_sections.punchline: Match rate to the payment period before applying PV = C / r: semi-annual payment needs the semi-annual rate.
explanation_sections.approach: Name the formula PV = C / r (perpetuity). Identify: C = Rs 9,000 per half-year, compounding semi-annual at 12% p.a. Semi-annual rate r = 12% / 2 = 6% = 0.06. PV = 9000 / 0.06 = 1,50,000.
explanation_sections.lesson: Always match the payment frequency to the rate frequency before applying C / r. An annual rate divided by compounding periods gives the per-period rate.
explanation_sections.timing: 30 seconds. The trap is using 12% instead of 6%. If your answer is 75,000 you used the annual rate directly.
